objectives: Reason about diffraction limits + beam quality.

slides.title: Gaussian beams: the basic free-space mode
slides.body:
Laser output beams are well-described as **Gaussian beams** — a specific transverse mode with Gaussian-intensity profile. Solution of paraxial Helmholtz equation:

  I(r, z) = I₀ (w₀/w(z))² exp(-2 r² / w(z)²)

with:
- **Waist** w₀: minimum radius (1/e² intensity) at z = 0.
- **Beam radius w(z)** = w₀ √(1 + (z/z_R)²).
- **Rayleigh length** z_R = π w₀² / λ.
- **Divergence half-angle** θ = λ / (π w₀) (far-field).
- **Radius of curvature** R(z) = z (1 + (z_R/z)²).
- **Gouy phase** Φ(z) = arctan(z/z_R).

**Key intuition**:
- Tight focus (small w₀) → short Rayleigh range + fast divergence.
- Collimated (large w₀) → long Rayleigh + slow divergence.
- Product w₀ × θ = λ/π is a beam-quality invariant.

**M² (beam-quality factor)**:
- M² = 1: perfect TEM_00 (Gaussian).
- M² > 1: real-world beams. He-Ne lasers ~ 1.05; high-power solid-state ~1.3; multimode fiber ~10-100.
- Effective divergence θ = M² × λ / (π w₀).
- Tight focusing limit: spot size ∝ M² × λ × f-number.

**Higher-order modes**: TEM_mn — Hermite-Gaussian (rectangular symmetry) or Laguerre-Gaussian (cylindrical). Cavities + fibers can support multiple modes. Donut beam (LG_01) carries orbital angular momentum.

slides.title: Diffraction: Fraunhofer + the limit of resolution
slides.body:
**Huygens-Fresnel principle**: each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary spherical wavelets. Net wave = superposition. Underlies all diffraction + interference.

**Fraunhofer (far-field) diffraction** of an aperture of size D: spot size on a screen at distance z is θ × z ≈ (λ / D) × z. So light cannot be confined to angular spread smaller than ~ λ/D.

**Examples**:
- Single slit (width a): central maximum width ~ 2λ/a. First null at sin θ = λ/a.
- Circular aperture (diameter D): Airy disk; first null at sin θ = 1.22 λ/D.
- N-slit grating: principal maxima at d sin θ = mλ; spectrometer dispersion.

**Abbe diffraction limit**: minimum resolvable feature ~ λ / (2 NA), where NA = n sin α (numerical aperture of focusing optic). For visible (λ = 500 nm) + immersion microscopy (NA = 1.4): ~180 nm — sub-wavelength diffraction limit.

**Beating the diffraction limit** (super-resolution):
- STED, PALM/STORM, SIM: fluorescence techniques exploiting nonlinearity to reach ~20-50 nm. (Hell + Betzig + Moerner, Nobel 2014.)
- Near-field (NSOM): probe within ~λ/10 of surface.
- Electron + X-ray microscopy: shorter λ → finer resolution.
- Plasmonics + metamaterials: sub-wavelength imaging in specific regimes.

**Photolithography wavelength evolution**:
- 248 nm (KrF excimer): 130 nm features.
- 193 nm (ArF excimer) + immersion + double patterning: 22-10 nm features.
- 13.5 nm EUV (extreme UV): current leading-edge (TSMC 3nm, 2nm in development).
- Computational lithography: optical proximity correction, source-mask optimization.

Each generation of EUV requires order-of-magnitude infrastructure improvement: laser-produced plasma source, multilayer Mo/Si reflective optics, all-vacuum operation, ~$200M lithography tools (ASML).

slides.title: Imaging + Fourier optics
slides.body:
**Fourier optics** (Goodman 1968 textbook): treat optical systems as Fourier transformers. Free-space propagation = phase shift in spatial-frequency domain. Thin lens = spatial Fourier transform between front + back focal planes.

**Key results**:
- Diffraction pattern of an aperture is its Fourier transform.
- Image at back focal plane of a lens = Fourier transform of object at front focal plane.
- 4-f imaging system: two lenses spaced by 4f; image is inverted; can manipulate Fourier plane between for filtering.
- Spatial filtering: block high frequencies in Fourier plane → low-pass (smooth) image; block DC → edge detection.
- Coherent vs incoherent imaging: coherent = amplitude; incoherent = intensity (averages over phase fluctuations).

**Modulation transfer function (MTF)**: how an optical system attenuates spatial frequencies. Used to characterize: lenses, cameras, displays, image-sensor systems.

**Computational imaging**:
- Coded apertures (single-pixel cameras, ghost imaging).
- Plenoptic cameras (light-field).
- Phase retrieval (in-line holography, ptychography).
- Computational lithography (OPC, ILT, source-mask optimization).
- ML-driven image reconstruction (deep deconvolution; SR; denoising).

**Holography** (Gabor 1948, Nobel 1971): record interference pattern of object beam + reference beam on photosensitive medium. Replay with reference reconstructs 3D image. Modern: digital holography (CMOS + computation), dynamic holographic displays (research).

question.question: Design a Gaussian-beam focusing system
question.goal: A 1 mm-diameter collimated laser at λ=1064 nm needs to be focused to a 10 µm spot. What focal length lens is needed?

steps.reveal: w_in = 0.5 mm = 500 µm (assumed Gaussian intensity profile; w₀ at 1/e²).

steps.prompt: For a Gaussian beam at the back focal plane of a lens, w_focus ≈ λ f / (π w_in). Solve for f.
hints: f = π w_in w_focus / λ = π × 5e-4 × 5e-6 / 1064e-9.
NA = w_in / f for thin lens.
steps.reveal: NA = w_in / f ≈ 500e-6 / 7.4e-3 ≈ 0.068. Modest NA; readily achievable with off-the-shelf optics. For tighter focus (e.g., to 1 µm spot), would need ~0.5 NA microscope objective.

z_R = π × (5e-6)² / 1064e-9 ≈ 73.8 µm. Focal-spot region: roughly 2 × z_R ≈ 150 µm depth-of-field. Tight focus → short depth-of-field — standard trade-off in laser cutting, photolithography, microscopy.

question.question: Drag to the diffraction-limited spot size (in nm) for visible light (λ = 500 nm) through a high-NA microscope objective (NA = 1.4).
question.explanation: Abbe diffraction limit: d ≈ λ / (2 NA) = 500 / 2.8 ≈ 180 nm. Real microscope objectives achieve ~200-250 nm in practice (limited by other factors). Super-resolution (STED, PALM/STORM, SIM): 20-100 nm via nonlinear fluorescence techniques. Electron microscopy: ~0.1 nm via λ ~ 0.01 nm electrons. X-ray microscopy: ~10 nm.

question.question: Why is M² (beam-quality factor) such a critical metric for industrial + scientific lasers?
options: M² quantifies how close a real beam is to ideal Gaussian. M² ≈ 1: tightly focusable, well-collimated; M² > 1: cannot be focused to diffraction-limited spot. Tight focus limit scales as M². For laser cutting / drilling / micromachining / surgery / photolithography, brightness (power × beam-quality) drives processing speed + precision. M² determines: minimum spot size achievable; maximum standoff distance for collimated delivery; coupling efficiency into single-mode fiber; resolution in laser-scanning systems.
question.explanation:
**M² (beam-quality factor)**:

*Definition*: ratio of beam-divergence × waist product to the ideal-Gaussian product (λ/π). M² = 1 means ideal TEM_00 mode.

*Real values*:
- Single-mode He-Ne laser: ~1.05.
- Diode-pumped solid-state (DPSS) Nd:YAG: ~1.1-1.3.
- Fiber laser, single-mode: ~1.05.
- High-power industrial fiber laser (multi-mode): ~1.5-3.
- Multimode fiber-coupled diode: ~10-100.
- High-power CO₂ laser: ~1.1-1.5.

*Why it matters*:

1. **Tight focusing**:
  Spot size ∝ M² × λ × f-number
  Higher M² → larger spot at given lens. For laser cutting: smaller spot = higher intensity = faster cutting + finer features.

2. **Standoff working distance**:
  Collimation maintained for ~ Rayleigh range × M². Higher M² → shorter usable beam path. Laser welding, marking, surface treatment.

3. **Single-mode fiber coupling**:
  Efficient only for M² ~ 1. Multimode beams couple to multimode fiber (with mode-scrambling issues) or require complex shaping.

4. **Scanning-system resolution**:
  In laser-scanning microscopy + photolithography: M² determines spot size + resolution + depth of focus.

5. **Beam combining**:
  Spectral or coherent combining of many lasers preserves total power only when sub-beams have good M². Cooler-running multimode beams sacrifice quality for power.

*Brightness*: P / (λ² × M⁴) — figure of merit combining power + quality. Determines processing rate in industrial laser systems. Recent improvements: high-power single-mode fiber lasers (IPG, Coherent) achieved 100s-kW at M² ~ 1.3 — game-changer for laser cutting + welding.

*Trade-offs*:
- Increasing power often degrades M² (thermal lensing, multimode oscillation).
- Active beam-shaping (deformable mirrors, mode-cleaning fiber) restores quality at cost of power.
- Different applications value M² vs raw power vs cost differently.

Industrial laser specs always include M² alongside power; without M², power figures alone are misleading.

slides.workedSolution: M² (beam-quality factor): ratio of real beam parameter product to ideal Gaussian. M² = 1 = ideal; M² > 1 = degraded focusability. Tight focus + collimation + fiber coupling + scanning resolution all scale with M². Brightness P/(λ² M⁴) is the figure of merit for industrial laser applications. Modern high-power single-mode fiber lasers (M²~1.3 at >100 kW) revolutionized laser cutting/welding by maintaining both power + quality.

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why the diffraction limit is both a fundamental constraint + a useful design tool.
question.rubric: Mentions: Abbe diffraction limit d ~ λ / (2 NA) sets fundamental spot size for far-field imaging + focusing. Constraint: cannot focus light tighter than ~λ/2 with normal optics. Design implication: shorter λ + higher NA give finer resolution → semiconductor lithography moved from 365 nm → 248 nm → 193 nm → 13.5 nm EUV (each generation reduces feature size). Microscopy: oil-immersion (NA 1.4 → 250 nm); super-resolution techniques exploit nonlinearity to bypass via switchable fluorophores. Modern photolithography: 193nm + multiple patterning + EUV + computational reach ~3-2 nm transistor features. Beyond diffraction: near-field, electron + X-ray. Concludes: diffraction is fundamental constraint that drives wavelength + NA engineering; super-resolution is loophole; entire semiconductor industry organized around continued battle.
